intro: Some traditions have no single written book. In a Yoruba town, a priest recites verses he learned by heart. In a Great Lakes community, an elder tells a story only in winter. In New Zealand, a Maori family welcomes guests with a chant. This unit begins with Indigenous traditions of Africa, the Americas and the Pacific, and how they survived hard times.

Then the unit turns to a question every country faces. How can people with different beliefs, and people with none, live together? You will read the First Amendment, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and cases from the Supreme Court. You will visit Chicago's 1893 Parliament of Religions and look at how researchers count the world's faiths.

By the end, you will be able to explain oral tradition, name specific nations and their practices, describe the two religion clauses, read a chart of estimates with care, and disagree about religion with respect.
bigQuestion: How do traditions survive being pushed aside, and how can people of every belief and none share one country?

timeline.t: The transatlantic slave trade carries African traditions to the Americas
The First Amendment protects religious freedom in the United States
The Treaty of Chicago; the Potawatomi are soon forced west
The Code of Indian Offenses bans many Native ceremonies
The World's Parliament of Religions meets in Chicago
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights names freedom of religion
The Bahá'í House of Worship in Wilmette is dedicated
The American Indian Religious Freedom Act is passed
The Supreme Court decides the Lukumi case; a new Parliament meets in Chicago
The UN adopts the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples

words.d: teachings, stories and history passed on by speaking and listening rather than by writing
in Yoruba tradition, spirit beings who each watch over part of nature and human life
a people scattered far from their homeland, and the communities they form
a people with its own government; U.S. law recognizes tribal nations this way
pressure on a group to give up its own culture and take on the majority culture
in Polynesian traditions, set apart as sacred or restricted
the proper way of doing something according to a community's rules
the part of the First Amendment that keeps government from setting up or favoring a religion
the part of the First Amendment that protects a person's right to practice their religion
harming or punishing people because of their religion, beliefs or identity
many different groups living side by side and taking part in shared public life
people who do not belong to any religion; sometimes called nones

choices: A book kept in a temple
Teachings passed on by voice, song and ceremony
test.why: Oral tradition passes on teachings by speaking and listening, as in many Indigenous traditions.

test.q: Osun, Ogun and Sango belong to which tradition?
test.why: Osun, Ogun and Sango are orisha in Yoruba tradition.

test.q: Candomble took shape in which country?
test.why: Candomble took shape in Brazil, especially Bahia.

test.q: What are the Seven Grandfather Teachings?
choices: Laws in the Bill of Rights
Anishinaabe teachings such as wisdom, respect and humility
test.why: The Seven Grandfather Teachings are Anishinaabe: wisdom, love, respect, bravery, honesty, humility and truth.

test.q: What did the American Indian Religious Freedom Act of 1978 state?
choices: A ban on the Sun Dance
A policy of protecting Native religious practice
test.why: The 1978 law stated U.S. policy to protect Native American religious practice.

test.q: The English word taboo comes from which idea?
test.why: Taboo comes from the Polynesian word tapu, meaning set apart or restricted.

test.q: Which is a respectful way to learn about a Native ceremony?
choices: Assume every nation does it the same way
Follow the community's protocol and name the nation
test.why: Respect means following protocol and naming the specific nation.

test.q: A state names one church as its official religion. Which clause does this break?
test.why: The Establishment Clause keeps government from setting up an official religion.

test.q: Which case protected Jehovah's Witness students who would not salute the flag?
test.why: In Barnette (1943), the Court ruled schools could not force the flag salute.

test.q: Which public school activity is allowed?
choices: Teaching what Sikhs believe about the Guru Granth Sahib
test.why: Schools may teach about religion objectively but may not practice or promote it.

test.q: Article 18 of the Universal Declaration includes which right?
choices: To change one's religion or belief
test.why: Article 18 includes the freedom to change one's religion or belief.

test.q: Who began his 1893 Chicago speech with 'Sisters and brothers of America'?
test.why: Swami Vivekananda, a Hindu monk, opened his speech this way at the 1893 Parliament.

test.q: Why should readers check who made a chart of world religions?
choices: Because counts are estimates that depend on definitions and methods
test.why: Religious counts are estimates; the source, year and definitions shape the numbers.

test.q: Which word fits a person who says no one can know whether God exists?
test.why: An agnostic holds that people cannot know whether God exists.

test.q: Which idea is found in Matthew 7:12, the Talmud's Hillel story and the Analects?
choices: A version of the Golden Rule
test.why: All three contain a version of treating others as you would want to be treated.

write.prompt: How should a country protect the religious lives of people who believe very different things? Use at least two sources from this unit, such as the First Amendment, the 1978 American Indian Religious Freedom Act, Article 18 or Matthew 7:12. Explain what each source says and how it helps answer the question.
tips: Name each source you cite, with its year.
Attribute every belief: say 'many Ojibwe people believe', not 'people believe'.
Name specific nations and traditions, not one general group.
Compare sources rather than judging any religion as right or wrong.
Use unit terms such as free exercise, protocol and pluralism.
